content: Erythema multiforme is a dermatological condition of uncertain origin. Some researchers propose that it is caused by the deposition of immune complexes, primarily immunoglobulin M (IgM), within the superficial microvasculature of the skin and oral mucosa. This condition can be triggered by drug exposure or associated with certain infections. Erythema multiforme presents in a spectrum of severity. The mild form, known as erythema multiforme minor, is typically a self-limiting rash. In contrast, the severe form, referred to as erythema multiforme major or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, can be life-threatening and involves mucosal surfaces. Drug reactions are a common cause of erythema multiforme. Medications such as sulfa drugs, hydrochlorothiazide, phenytoin, barbiturates, penicillin, allopurinol, ethynodiol diacetate, and ethinyl estradiol are frequently implicated. Additionally, internal medical conditions may contribute to its development. Among infections, herpes simplex virus is the most common predisposing factor, though bacterial infections (notably Mycoplasma) and fungal diseases are also associated. The cutaneous form of erythema multiforme, which is more prevalent than the severe form, typically manifests as mildly pruritic, pink-red blotches that are symmetrically distributed, often beginning on the extremities. These lesions frequently exhibit the characteristic target lesion appearance, with a pink-red ring surrounding a pale center. The condition generally resolves within 7 to 10 days. Laboratory findings in erythema multiforme are non-specific. They may include an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), increased white blood cell count (WBC), and elevated liver enzyme levels.
